name: Jungian Individuation
line: Meet your shadow through dreams and symbols.

quote.text: Who looks outside, dreams; who looks inside, awakes.

quotes.text: One does not become enlightened by imagining figures of light, but by making the darkness conscious.
When an inner situation is not made conscious, it happens outside, as fate.
The dream is a little hidden door in the innermost and most secret recesses of the soul.
quotes.source: The Meaning of Psychology for Modern Man, 1933

quotes.text: Everything that irritates us about others can lead us to an understanding of ourselves.
The meeting of two personalities is like the contact of two chemical substances: if there is any reaction, both are transformed.
quotes.source: Modern Man in Search of a Soul, 1933

quotes.text: The sole purpose of human existence is to kindle a light in the darkness of mere being.

words.meaning: Becoming whole; becoming who you are
words.usage: The lifelong work of bringing conscious and unconscious into relation.

words.meaning: What you disown in yourself
words.usage: Not only the bad. Whatever did not fit the person you needed to be.

words.meaning: The mask you show the world
words.usage: The Roman actor’s mask. Necessary, and dangerous to mistake for your face.

words.meaning: The inner feminine figure in a man
words.usage: Jung’s term; later Jungians treat it less by gender and more as the inner other.

words.meaning: The inner masculine figure in a woman
words.usage: The counterpart of the anima.

words.meaning: The centre and the whole of the psyche
words.usage: Written with a capital. Larger than the ego, which is only the centre of consciousness.

words.meaning: The centre of the conscious mind
words.usage: The "I" that thinks it runs the house.

words.meaning: An inherited pattern of experience
words.usage: Mother, child, trickster, wise old man. The pattern is inherited; the images are not.

words.meaning: The layer of the psyche shared by all people
words.usage: Deeper than personal memory, and the source of myths.

words.meaning: A charged cluster of feelings and memories
words.usage: Jung: people do not have complexes; complexes have them.

words.meaning: Seeing your own contents in someone else
words.usage: It happens to you; you do not do it. The clue is disproportionate emotion.

words.meaning: A meaningful coincidence
words.usage: An inner and an outer event that match in meaning, with no causal link.

words.meaning: A waking dialogue with inner figures
words.usage: Let an image move, then engage it as real. Jung’s chief method after 1913.

words.meaning: Enlarging a dream image through myth and symbol
words.usage: Ask not only what it reminds you of, but where humanity has met it before.

words.meaning: A thing turning into its opposite
words.usage: From Heraclitus. Any extreme calls up its contrary.

words.meaning: Charged with a sense of the sacred
words.usage: Rudolf Otto’s word. Fascinating and frightening at once.

words.meaning: A circle; an image of wholeness
words.usage: Jung drew one each morning in 1918–19 and found they tracked his inner state.

words.meaning: A protected sacred space
words.usage: The marked-off precinct of a temple. The analytic hour is one.

words.meaning: The union of opposites
words.usage: The alchemists’ royal marriage. Jung read it as a picture of inner integration.

words.meaning: The blackening
words.usage: First stage of the alchemical work: darkness, confusion, the meeting with shadow.

words.meaning: The first matter
words.usage: The despised raw stuff the work begins with. It is found in the dung heap.

words.meaning: Psychic energy
words.usage: For Jung, life energy in general, not only sexual as for Freud.

words.meaning: The whole of the mind, conscious and unconscious
words.usage: Jung insisted it is as real as the body.

words.meaning: The unconscious balancing a one-sided attitude
words.usage: Dreams usually show what the day left out.

words.meaning: The third thing that arises when opposites are held
words.usage: Do not choose too soon. Stay in the tension and a symbol appears.

words.meaning: The ego puffed up by identifying with an archetype
words.usage: Feeling chosen, or feeling uniquely worthless. Both are inflation.

words.meaning: Energy turned toward the inner world
words.usage: With extraversion, the pair he introduced in Psychological Types.

words.meaning: The archetype of disorder and reversal
words.usage: Hermes, Loki, the fool. The one who upsets what has grown rigid.

words.meaning: The eternal youth
words.usage: Charm, promise, and a refusal to land.

words.meaning: The night-sea journey; descent to the underworld
words.usage: From the Odyssey. Jung’s name for a descent into the unconscious.

words.meaning: One world
words.usage: The alchemists’ idea that psyche and matter share a single ground.

words.meaning: A fourfold pattern of wholeness
words.usage: Four directions, four functions. Jung thought three always asks for a fourth.

practices.name: Record a dream
practices.instructions: Keep a notebook and pen by the bed. On waking, lie still and let the dream return before you move. Write it in the present tense, in order, without tidying it: setting, people, what happened, how it ended. Note the feeling on waking and anything from yesterday it touches. If there is no dream, write that, and write the mood you woke in.
practices.why: For Jung the dream is not a disguise. It is a spontaneous self-portrait of the psyche, showing what the conscious view is leaving out.
variations: Give the dream a title.
Sketch its central image.
List your own associations to each element before reaching for any dictionary of symbols.

practices.name: Inner weather
practices.instructions: Sit with your coffee or tea and ask: what is the weather inside me this morning? Not what it should be, what it is. Sunny, foggy, stormy, still? Write it as a short forecast: a mood, a colour, a sentence. Do not try to change it. Only notice, and check at noon to see how it has moved.
practices.why: Jung said the first step in any inner work is to see what is there without a verdict. A weather report is a gentle, even playful, way to do it.
variations: Name the weather in a single colour.
Draw it as a small sketch.
Report it to a friend in one line.

practices.name: Draw the dream image
practices.instructions: Take the most vivid image from last night’s dream, or any image that has stayed with you, and draw it. It does not have to look good. Use whatever pen or colours are at hand. Look at it when you have finished. Is anything different from what you had in mind? Add one more detail and stop.
practices.why: Jung painted and carved his own images, and had his patients do the same. Drawing slows the image down, so you see more than you did when it simply floated past.
variations: Draw with your other hand.
Draw it three times, each a little differently.
Paint it with whatever colour you have.

practices.name: Walk by water
practices.instructions: Walk beside water, a lake, a river, the sea, a canal, and let your mind drift. When an image arises, note it. Do not analyse, and do not hurry. If there is no water nearby, walk where the ground is wet or watch rain. Jung lived his entire adult life on the shore of Lake Zurich, and walked and wrote there.
practices.why: Water has always been the common image for the unconscious. A walk beside it is a way to let thoughts rise up on their own, without prompting.
variations: Carry a notebook and write only one line.
Throw a stone in and watch the rings.
Walk in silence with someone.

practices.name: Build with your hands
practices.instructions: Stack stones, make a tower of blocks, shape clay, or build something small from whatever is at hand. Do not plan it. Let your hands decide and notice what comes. Then step back. Jung went back to a childhood game of building in his crisis of 1912, and it started his inner work again.
practices.why: After his break with Freud, Jung found himself stuck until he allowed himself to play with stones by the lake. The play released images and fantasies that became the Red Book.
variations: Build outdoors with natural things.
Build something and take it apart.
Build with a child and follow their lead.

practices.name: Check your mask
practices.instructions: As you get ready, ask: which face am I going to wear today? The professional, the cheerful friend, the competent parent? Name it, with a smile. Persona is not a lie, it is a useful costume. Then ask: what in me does this mask hide, and what would I like it to show? Decide one small thing to let through.
practices.why: Jung called the mask we show the world the persona. It is necessary, and it becomes a problem only when we forget we are wearing one.
variations: Name a different persona for each place you go.
Wear one thing today that shows a hidden side.
Ask a friend which mask they see most.

practices.name: Amplify an image
practices.instructions: Take one image from a dream, a daydream or something that caught your eye today. Write it in the middle of a page. Around it, write every association that comes: personal memories first, then stories, myths or pictures it reminds you of. Do not interpret. Finish by asking: what does this image want me to look at?
practices.why: Jung called this amplification: staying with an image and widening it, rather than reducing it to a single meaning. It keeps the unconscious speaking and the ego listening.
variations: Draw the image instead of writing.
Use a figure from a fairy tale.
Share it with someone you trust.

practices.name: Active imagination
practices.instructions: Sit alone and undisturbed. Take an image from a dream, or the feeling of a mood, and hold it in attention until it begins to move by itself. Do not direct it. When a figure appears, speak to it and let it answer; write the exchange down as it happens. Treat what it says as you would a person’s words. End deliberately: close the notebook, stand up, and do something ordinary. Stop if it feels overwhelming.
practices.why: Jung developed the method during his own crisis after 1913 and recorded it in the Red Book. It lets the unconscious speak and requires the ego to answer.
variations: Paint or model the image in clay instead of writing.
Continue a dream from where it broke off.
Ask a recurring mood: who are you, and what do you want?

practices.name: Catch a projection
practices.instructions: Think of one strong reaction today, a flash of irritation, envy or admiration. Ask: what am I seeing in them that I do not see in myself? Write down the quality in a word. Then ask: when have I been like that, or wanted to be? Withdrawing a projection is the daily work of knowing yourself, and it makes others easier to bear.
practices.why: Jung held that what we cannot see in ourselves we meet in other people, with a charge. A few honest minutes of this a day is one of the most useful habits in his whole approach.
variations: Do it for someone you admire.
Do it for a public figure.
Do it for a character in a film.

practices.name: Collect a coincidence
practices.instructions: Notice any meaningful coincidence today: a name you just heard on the radio, a number you keep seeing, a song at the right moment. Write it down in one line, with the time. Do not explain it or decide what it means. Only collect. After a week, read the list and see if a pattern emerges.
practices.why: Jung named such events synchronicity, a meaningful coincidence without a causal link. He kept a record of them, and he saw their value as pointers rather than proofs.
variations: Keep the list on your phone.
Share a coincidence with a friend.
Look for the one that surprised you most.

practices.name: Find yourself in a fairy tale
practices.instructions: Read a short fairy tale, one of Grimm’s or any you like, and ask which character you are today: the hero, the helper, the trickster, the villain, the bystander. Notice which one you resist. Write one line about what that figure wants. Fairy tales, said Jung’s colleague von Franz, are the simplest expressions of the psyche.
practices.why: Marie-Louise von Franz spent her life on fairy tales, because their figures are simple and universal. They are the best way to meet archetypes without a lecture.
variations: Read it aloud to a child.
Choose the character you like least.
Rewrite the ending the way you wish.

practices.name: Do something physical
practices.instructions: After inner work, do something with your body: chop vegetables, wash the car, dig a bed, split wood, scrub the floor. Do it fully, without screens. Jung chopped wood and cooked at his tower for exactly this reason: to bring the inner material down into the hands and feet. Feel the weight come back.
practices.why: The last rule of this Onda is to follow inner work with something physical. It grounds the mind and keeps the images from swamping the day.
variations: Walk fast for fifteen minutes.
Cook something with your hands.
Tidy a room from top to bottom.

practices.name: Shadow note
practices.instructions: Think of one person who provoked a strong reaction in you today: irritation, contempt, envy or fascination. Write down exactly what quality set you off, in a few adjectives. Then ask honestly: where does this live in me? When have I been this, wanted to be this, or forbidden myself this? Write what you find. No conclusions are needed.
practices.why: What we cannot see in ourselves we meet in other people, with a charge. Withdrawing a projection is, for Jung, the first real act of moral work.
variations: Do the same for someone you admire: what are you giving away?
Write a short letter from your shadow to you.
Note what you were proudest of today, and what that pride needs you not to be.

practices.name: Draw a mandala
practices.instructions: Draw a circle that fills the page. Starting at the centre and working outward, fill it with whatever shapes and colours come, without planning or judging. When it feels finished, date it and write one line beneath. Do not interpret it tonight. Keep the drawings together and look back over them at the end of the week.
practices.why: While stationed as a camp commandant in 1918 and 1919, Jung sketched a small circular drawing each morning and saw that it changed with his inner state. He called the circle the image of wholeness.
variations: Use only one colour.
Make it from stones or leaves outdoors.
Draw it with your non-writing hand.

practices.name: The last hour, unscrolled
practices.instructions: For the last hour before sleep, put away the phone and every screen. Do something slow: read on paper, tidy, listen to music, sit with a lamp. Notice what comes up when nothing is feeding you. Boredom, a worry, a picture. That is the material this Onda is about, and it needs a quiet hour to arrive.
practices.why: The rule of this Onda is to leave the last hour before sleep unscrolled. Jung believed the unconscious speaks most clearly when the mind is not occupied by noise.
variations: Start with thirty minutes if an hour is too much.
Charge the phone in another room.
Use the hour to write by hand.

practices.name: Ask the dream a question
practices.instructions: Before you sleep, write a question on a slip of paper or in your notebook: what do I need to see about this situation? Read it, put the notebook by the bed, and let it go. In the morning, write down whatever dream or image you have, and see whether it touches the question. Some nights nothing comes. That is also an answer.
practices.why: Asking the dreams a question before sleep is an old practice, often called dream incubation. Jung recommended it when a problem seemed to have no answer in waking life.
variations: Ask a very small question.
Ask the same question three nights running.
Ask a question for someone else.

practices.name: Tea and the notebook
practices.instructions: Make a pot of herbal tea, lime blossom or verbena, and sit with your notebook. Write anything: a line, a list, a sketch, a complaint. Do not read it back. Let the tea cool a little as you write. It is a small, unhurried way to end the day with yourself, a bit like a conversation with an old friend.
practices.why: The notebook is the Jungian’s constant companion. A cup of herbal tea beside it makes it a pleasure and not a duty.
variations: Write a single sentence only.
Write with a different pen.
Write to the person you were this morning.

practices.name: Go to your corner
practices.instructions: Choose a corner, a chair or a desk and keep it as a place apart. Sit there for ten minutes with nothing in your hands. At Bollingen, Jung had a room that he alone entered. Anyone can have a small version: a place where the day’s noise does not follow. Sit, breathe, and be with whatever arrives.
practices.why: The Greeks called a sacred precinct a temenos, a protected space. Jung used the word for the sealed, safe space in which inner work can happen.
variations: Add a candle.
Keep it as the place where you read and write.
Mark it with a stone or a flower.

practices.name: A day at the tower
practices.instructions: On a free afternoon, live a little like Jung at his stone tower. Cook a slow stew, on a wood stove if you can, or simply take hours over it. Chop the wood, stir the pot, light a lamp. No screens, no hurry, no schedule. Eat late and slowly. He said he felt most himself when he did these plain things.
practices.why: Jung built Bollingen Tower from 1923, with his own hands, as a place to live simply: no electricity, a wood stove, a lake. He said that there he was in the midst of his true life.
variations: Do it with a friend and share the stew.
Do it with one candle and no other light.
Do it in a garden, with an open fire if safe.

practices.name: Sit with the dark
practices.instructions: At night, put out the lights and sit in a dark room, with one candle if you want. For fifteen minutes just sit. Notice what the dark brings: shapes, memories, a small fear, a deeper calm. Jung called the descent into darkness the night-sea journey. Stop and turn on the light whenever you wish; nothing needs to be endured.
practices.why: The nekyia, the night-sea journey, is Jung’s name for the descent into the unconscious, where the sun disappears so that it can rise again. You can feel a small version of it in a dark room.
variations: Do it outdoors under the stars.
Do it with a friend, in silence.
Do it and write what came afterwards.

immersePlan.name: Read a chapter of Man and His Symbols
immersePlan.text: Open the one book Jung wrote for general readers, finished days before he died. Read a short chapter, and notice which image, a tree, a house, a circle, sets your own memory moving.

immersePlan.name: Read about Jung’s childhood
immersePlan.text: Read the early chapters of Jung’s autobiography, in which he describes his childhood visions. Notice what he writes about being alone with a thought, and what made him feel safe.

immersePlan.name: Read a chapter of Inner Work
immersePlan.text: Read a chapter of Robert A. Johnson’s clear, step-by-step guide to dreams and active imagination. Try one small exercise from it today, and stop if it feels like too much.

immersePlan.name: Watch Jung at eighty-four
immersePlan.text: Find the 1959 BBC interview in which John Freeman talks with Jung at his home. Watch how an old man listens, and how he answers when asked if he believes in God.

immersePlan.name: Watch A Dangerous Method
immersePlan.text: Watch Cronenberg’s film of Jung, Freud and Sabina Spielrein. It is a dramatisation with liberties, so enjoy it as a story. Notice how each man handles the strange thing they have found.

immersePlan.name: Watch a dream being worked
immersePlan.text: Watch part of the film in which Marie-Louise von Franz, Jung’s closest collaborator, works on ordinary people’s dreams. Notice how she asks questions and keeps the dream open.

immersePlan.name: Listen to In Our Time on Jung
immersePlan.text: Put on the BBC discussion of Jung’s life, his ideas and his split from Freud. Listen on a walk, and note one idea you want to look into further.

immersePlan.name: Hear an episode of This Jungian Life
immersePlan.text: Play a podcast episode in which three Jungian analysts work on a listener’s dream. Try to guess the meaning before they say it, then compare.

immersePlan.name: Play The Rhythm of the Heat
immersePlan.text: Play Peter Gabriel’s song about Jung’s night among drummers in East Africa. Listen for the moment it speeds up. Ask what the music is doing that words cannot.

immersePlan.name: Look at the Red Book illuminations
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of pages from the Red Book: dragons, trees, mandalas, the figure of Philemon. Choose the page you like least, and stay with it for two minutes.

immersePlan.name: Look at the alchemical Rosarium
immersePlan.text: Look at the sixteenth-century woodcuts in which a king and queen meet, merge, die and are reborn. Jung used the series to talk about the stages of a relationship. Find the one that matches where you are.

immersePlan.name: Look at Blake’s plates
immersePlan.text: Look at a plate or two of Blake’s Songs, words and pictures from a poet who spoke with his own inner figures. Read a poem aloud and notice what the picture adds.

immersePlan.name: Make rösti
immersePlan.text: Grate cooked potatoes, press them into a pan and fry slowly in butter until crisp on both sides. It is the Swiss supper Jung would have known. Eat it with an apple or a green salad.

immersePlan.name: Eat dark bread and cheese
immersePlan.text: Have a plain Swiss supper of dark bread, cheese and an apple. Eat it slowly, at a table, with the notebook closed. Notice how nourishing simple things can be.

immersePlan.name: Make Bircher muesli
immersePlan.text: Soak oats overnight, then stir in grated apple, nuts and lemon. It was invented about 1900 by a Zurich physician, a few streets from where Jung worked. Eat it slowly in the morning.

immersePlan.name: Drink lime blossom tea
immersePlan.text: Make a cup of lime blossom or verbena tea, and sit with the notebook. Write down whatever comes. It is a drink for evening and quiet.

immersePlan.name: Drink one glass, attended to
immersePlan.text: If you drink, have one glass of wine with dinner and attend to it: colour, smell, taste, finish. If not, do the same with a glass of juice. One thing, fully.

immersePlan.name: Drink a glass of cold water
immersePlan.text: Pour a glass of plain water and drink it as if you had pumped it by hand. At the tower, Jung had no running water. Notice what it takes for the water to arrive in your glass.

immersePlan.name: Set up a dream notebook
immersePlan.text: Put a notebook and pen by your bed tonight. Write the date and a single question at the top of a fresh page. In the morning, write before you move, even a scrap.

immersePlan.name: Walk beside water
immersePlan.text: Walk beside a lake, a river or the sea, as Jung did all his adult life on the shore of Lake Zurich. Let one image come, and do not try to name it.

immersePlan.name: Build with stones
immersePlan.text: Stack stones or build a little tower or wall with blocks or any hard shapes. Do not plan. Jung returned to building as a way to find his way back to his images.

immersePlan.name: Play Dixit
immersePlan.text: Play the card game of dreamlike pictures and one-line clues. Everyone finds a different meaning in the same picture, which is the whole point. Notice which card you were sure of, and who else saw it.

immersePlan.name: Play a little of Psychonauts
immersePlan.text: If you have the game, play a level and enjoy entering a mind as a world. Notice the emotional baggage drawn as luggage. If not, imagine a place that shows how your own mind looks today.

immersePlan.name: Look at Persona 5’s Jungian terms
immersePlan.text: Persona 5 takes its terms straight from Jung: each character must face a shadow and gain a persona. Play a little if you have it, or read a summary and see how the game borrows the ideas.

immersePlan.name: Keep Jung’s birthday
immersePlan.text: Jung was born on 26 July 1875, at Kesswil on Lake Constance. Mark any day by writing down one dream or image, and say who you are grateful to for teaching you to look inward.

immersePlan.name: Look at Jung’s house at Küsnacht
immersePlan.text: Look up the lakeside house at Küsnacht that Jung built in 1908 and lived in until his death. Find a photograph of his study and ask what your own study says about you.

immersePlan.name: Look at the cathedral of his vision
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of the cathedral in Basel, the setting of the childhood vision Jung describes in Memories, Dreams, Reflections. Notice how an ordinary building can hold a strange memory.

immersePlan.name: Meet the shadow in a word
immersePlan.text: Shadow is what you disown in yourself. Write down three qualities you find hard in other people. Next to each, write a quiet yes, I have a bit of that, and see if it softens.

immersePlan.name: Spot the persona
immersePlan.text: Persona is the mask you show the world. Notice how your voice, face and words change between a meeting, a call with a friend and a quiet moment alone. Name each persona in one word.

immersePlan.name: Look for synchronicity
immersePlan.text: Synchronicity is a meaningful coincidence. Keep an eye out today for one. When you find it, write it in one line and leave it unexplained.

rules.text: Write the dream before you do anything else
rules.why: Dreams fade within minutes of moving and speaking. The notebook comes before the phone.

rules.text: Describe the image; do not judge it
rules.why: Interpretation too early kills the symbol. Stay with what it looks like and what it does, the way you would with a stranger.
A strong reaction to another person is information about you first. Who got under your skin, and what were they carrying for you?

rules.text: Leave the last hour before sleep unscrolled
rules.why: Give the night something of your own to work on.
The work needs a closed vessel. Jung compared it to the sealed flask of the alchemists.

rules.text: Follow inner work with something physical
rules.why: Wash up, walk, chop vegetables. Jung insisted on a firm footing in ordinary life, and so should you.

read.why: The one book he wrote for general readers, finished days before he died.

read.title: Memories, Dreams, Reflections
read.creator: C. G. Jung, recorded by Aniela Jaffé
read.why: An autobiography of the inner life: childhood visions, the break with Freud, the tower.

read.title: Modern Man in Search of a Soul
read.creator: C. G. Jung
read.why: Essays on dreams, the stages of life and what therapy is for.

read.title: The Undiscovered Self
read.creator: C. G. Jung
read.why: A short, late warning about mass movements and the unexamined individual.

read.title: The Red Book: A Reader’s Edition
read.creator: C. G. Jung, ed. Sonu Shamdasani
read.why: His private record of visions and dialogues, kept from 1913 and unpublished for almost fifty years after his death.

read.title: Inner Work
read.creator: Robert A. Johnson
read.why: A clear, step-by-step guide to dreams and active imagination.

read.title: Owning Your Own Shadow
read.creator: Robert A. Johnson
read.why: A very short book on the dark side of the psyche.

read.title: Jung’s Map of the Soul
read.creator: Murray Stein
read.why: The best single introduction to the theory as a whole.

read.title: Demian
read.creator: Hermann Hesse
read.why: A novel written after Hesse’s analysis with a student of Jung.

watch.why: Jung at eighty-four, at home. Asked if he believes in God: "I don’t need to believe. I know."

watch.creator: Mark Whitney
watch.why: A documentary portrait built from interviews with people who knew him.

watch.creator: David Cronenberg
watch.why: Jung, Freud and Sabina Spielrein. A dramatisation, with liberties.

listen.why: His life, his ideas and his split from Freud.

listen.creator: Three Jungian analysts
listen.why: A weekly podcast that ends each episode by working on a listener’s dream.

listen.creator: The Police

listen.why: A song about Jung’s night among drummers in East Africa.

art.title: Systema Munditotius
art.creator: C. G. Jung
art.why: His first mandala: a map of the whole cosmos, inner and outer.

art.title: The Bollingen stone
art.creator: C. G. Jung
art.why: A cube he carved with Greek and Latin inscriptions for his seventy-fifth birthday.

art.title: Rosarium Philosophorum

art.why: King and queen meet, merge, die and are reborn. Jung used the series to explain relationship.

art.title: Songs of Innocence and of Experience
art.creator: William Blake
art.why: Words and images from a poet who spoke with his own inner figures.

eat.title: Rösti
eat.creator: Swiss fried potato cake
eat.why: Grated, pressed and fried slowly in butter until crisp.

eat.title: A slow stew
eat.creator: Cooked over a fire if you can
eat.why: Jung was a keen cook at Bollingen, where meals took hours on a wood stove.

eat.title: Bircher muesli
eat.creator: Oats, grated apple, nuts, lemon
eat.why: Devised around 1900 by a Zurich physician, a few streets from where Jung trained.

drink.title: Herbal tea
drink.creator: Lime blossom or verbena
drink.why: In the evening, with the notebook.

drink.title: Well water
drink.creator: Or plain water
drink.why: The tower had no running water. He pumped it by hand.

customs.why: The first minutes after waking are when the dream is still within reach.

customs.title: Build with stone
customs.creator: Or any slow handwork
customs.why: In his crisis of 1912–13 he went back to a childhood game of building with stones by the lake.

customs.title: Keep a place apart
customs.creator: A room, a desk, a corner
customs.why: At Bollingen he had a locked room he alone entered, with painted walls.

customs.title: Live simply for a few days
customs.creator: No electricity if possible
customs.why: At the tower he chopped wood, lit oil lamps and said he felt most himself.

games.title: Persona 5
games.creator: Video game · Atlus
games.why: The series takes its terms straight from Jung: each character must face a Shadow and awaken a Persona, and the last chapters go down into a collective unconscious.

games.title: Psychonauts
games.creator: Video game · Double Fine
games.why: You enter other people’s minds as worlds to explore, with emotional baggage to sort and inner censors to dodge. Funny, and kinder than it looks.

games.title: Dixit
games.creator: Card game · Jean-Louis Roubira
games.why: Dreamlike pictures and one-line clues. Everyone finds a different meaning in the same image, which is a fair lesson in projection.

games.title: Disco Elysium
games.creator: Video game · ZA/UM
games.why: A detective whose inner voices argue with him all day. Few games give so clear a picture of a psyche made of many parts.

festivals.title: Eranos gatherings
festivals.creator: Late summer, Ascona, Switzerland
festivals.why: Since 1933 scholars of religion, myth and science have met beside Lake Maggiore. Jung attended for years and tried out many of his ideas there.

festivals.title: Jung’s birthday
festivals.creator: 26 July
festivals.why: Born in 1875 at Kesswil on Lake Constance. A good day to record a dream in full.

festivals.title: International congress of analytical psychology
festivals.creator: Every three years
festivals.why: Jungian analysts from around the world meet in a different city. Public lectures run alongside.

places.title: C. G. Jung House Museum
places.creator: Küsnacht, near Zurich, Switzerland
places.why: The lakeside house Jung built in 1908 and lived in until his death. Guided visits show the library and consulting room.

places.title: Bollingen Tower
places.creator: Upper Lake Zurich, Switzerland
places.why: The stone tower Jung built with his own hands from 1923. It is private and still owned by the family, but can be seen from the shore path and the water.

places.title: Monte Verità and Eranos
places.creator: Ascona, Ticino, Switzerland
places.why: The hill of early twentieth-century reformers and, by the lake below, the house where the Eranos meetings are held.

places.title: Basel Minster
places.creator: Basel, Switzerland
places.why: The cathedral of the boyhood vision Jung describes in Memories, Dreams, Reflections. He went to school in its shadow.

places.title: Kesswil
places.creator: Thurgau, Switzerland
places.why: The village of his birth on Lake Constance, with a plaque on the parsonage where his father was pastor.

ethics.title: Own your shadow
ethics.text: What you refuse to see in yourself, you will meet in others and fight there. Taking it back is the beginning of ethics.
ethics.practice: Take back one accusation you made today and see how much of it is yours.

ethics.title: Become whole, not perfect
ethics.text: Perfection belongs to the gods. Completeness is the human task, and it includes the parts you would rather not have.
ethics.practice: Name one flaw you will stop hiding and start managing.

ethics.title: Take symbols seriously
ethics.text: A dream or fantasy is a fact of your psyche. It deserves the respect you would give any other fact.
ethics.practice: Do one small real thing in response to a dream.

ethics.title: Carry your own burden
ethics.text: Each person who withdraws a projection lifts a little weight off the world.
ethics.practice: Before blaming, ask what you contributed.

ethics.title: Stay in the tension
ethics.text: When two real obligations conflict, do not escape into one side. Holding both is what lets a third way appear.
ethics.practice: Leave one decision open another day.

ethics.title: Honour the second half of life
ethics.text: What was right at twenty is a lie at fifty. The afternoon of life has its own purpose, turned inward.
ethics.practice: Ask what your age is asking of you.

philosophy.title: The unconscious is not empty
philosophy.text: It is not just a cellar of what was repressed. It is older than consciousness, creative, and has its own aims.
philosophy.practice: Before a decision today, ask what the part of you that is not speaking wants.

philosophy.title: Archetypes
philosophy.text: Humans everywhere dream the same figures: mother, child, hero, trickster, wise elder. They are forms the psyche is born with.
philosophy.practice: Which figure has been running your week?

philosophy.title: The two halves of life
philosophy.text: The first half builds an ego and a place in the world. The second asks what it was all for, and turns toward the Self.
philosophy.practice: Which half are you living in? Which one are you still trying to live?

philosophy.title: Synchronicity
philosophy.text: Now and then an outer event answers an inner state so exactly that chance does not cover it. Jung thought psyche and world might be two faces of one thing.
philosophy.practice: Note one coincidence today without explaining it.

philosophy.title: Compensation
philosophy.text: The psyche regulates itself. Push too far in one direction and dreams, moods and accidents begin pushing back.
philosophy.practice: Where are you one-sided right now? What is the other side saying?

philosophy.title: Projection
philosophy.text: We do not see others as they are until we have seen what we put on them.
philosophy.practice: Pick one person and ask what they carry for you.

philosophy.title: The persona
philosophy.text: Everyone needs a face for the world. The trouble starts when you can no longer take it off.
philosophy.practice: Notice the moment you put the mask on today, and the moment you took it off.

philosophy.title: The Self
philosophy.text: There is a centre in you that is not the ego and knows more than it does. Individuation is the ego learning to serve it.
philosophy.practice: Recall a time something wiser than your plans steered you.

philosophy.title: Opposites
philosophy.text: Everything psychic comes in pairs. Consciousness grows by holding both ends, not by picking one.
philosophy.practice: Find the opposite of your strongest opinion and argue for it for a minute.

philosophy.title: Meaning
philosophy.text: People can bear almost any suffering if it has meaning, and almost none if it does not. Much unhappiness is a life too small for the soul.
philosophy.practice: What, today, felt meaningful? Do more of that.

intro: Individuation is Carl Jung’s name for the process of becoming the person you actually are: not better, not perfect, but whole. It is a psychology, not a religion, though Jung thought it answered the same need.

Jung was a Swiss psychiatrist, born in 1875, who began his career at the Burghölzli hospital in Zurich listening closely to what his patients’ delusions were about. He found patterns in them that recurred in myths the patients had never read. For six years he was Freud’s closest ally and intended heir. They parted in 1913, chiefly over Freud’s insistence that the unconscious is driven by sexuality and Jung’s conviction that it holds something larger.

What followed was a breakdown, or an experiment, or both. For several years Jung let fantasies rise while awake, talked with the figures that appeared, and wrote and painted the results in a great red folio. Out of that confrontation came nearly all his later ideas. There is a personal unconscious, made of what one has forgotten or pushed away. Beneath it lies a collective unconscious, common to everyone, structured by archetypes: inherited forms that shape experience and surface as the recurring figures of dream and myth.

Individuation is the gradual meeting with these. First comes the persona, the mask one wears, and behind it the shadow, everything about oneself that was unacceptable. Then the inner other, which Jung called anima or animus. At the centre is the Self, the organising whole of the personality, of which the conscious ego is only a part. The goal is not to conquer the unconscious but to come into relationship with it, so that life is lived from a centre larger than the ego’s wishes.

His methods are simple to state: write down your dreams and take them seriously; let images speak through active imagination; notice what you project onto other people and take it back; give the psyche form by drawing, painting, carving. He found confirmation for the process in unexpected places, above all in medieval alchemy, which he read as a symbolic account of inner transformation.

This Onda borrows those methods for a few weeks of self-observation. It is not therapy and does not replace one. Jung himself warned that the unconscious should be approached with respect and a firm footing in ordinary life. If the material that comes up is heavy, take it to a trained analyst or therapist.

figures.name: Carl Gustav Jung
figures.bio: Swiss psychiatrist and founder of analytical psychology.

figures.name: Emma Jung
figures.bio: His wife, an analyst and scholar in her own right. Spent thirty years on a study of the Grail legend.

figures.name: Sigmund Freud
figures.bio: Founder of psychoanalysis. Jung’s mentor from 1907 until their break in 1913.

figures.name: Toni Wolff
figures.bio: Analyst and Jung’s close collaborator through the Red Book years.

figures.name: Marie-Louise von Franz
figures.bio: His chief collaborator on alchemy and the leading interpreter of fairy tales.

figures.name: Richard Wilhelm
figures.bio: Translator of the I Ching and The Secret of the Golden Flower, which turned Jung toward alchemy.

figures.name: Wolfgang Pauli
figures.bio: Nobel physicist who worked with Jung on synchronicity.

figures.name: Aniela Jaffé
figures.bio: His secretary, who recorded and edited Memories, Dreams, Reflections.

figures.name: James Hillman
figures.bio: Founder of archetypal psychology, the most influential revision of Jung.

history.detail: Under Eugen Bleuler he studies schizophrenia and develops the word association test, which reveals emotionally charged "complexes".
They talk in Vienna for thirteen hours without a break. Freud soon names him "crown prince" of psychoanalysis.
Jung’s study of a young woman’s fantasies treats libido as general psychic energy and myth as its language. Freud cannot accept it.
Their correspondence ends in January. That autumn Jung has visions of Europe drowned in blood, and begins the inner experiment he later called his confrontation with the unconscious.

history.what: The first mandala and the first statement of method
history.detail: He paints Systema Munditotius and writes the essay on the transcendent function, describing active imagination.
Introduces introversion and extraversion and four functions: thinking, feeling, sensation, intuition.
After his mother’s death he begins building a stone tower by the upper lake, with his own hands, and adds to it over three decades.

history.what: Travels to Taos and East Africa
history.detail: Conversations with Ochwiay Biano of Taos Pueblo and months among the Elgonyi in Kenya shake his European assumptions.

history.what: The Secret of the Golden Flower
history.detail: Richard Wilhelm sends him a Chinese alchemical text. Jung recognises his own mandalas in it and turns to the study of alchemy.

The Eranos conferences begin at Ascona. The same year Jung becomes president of the International General Medical Society for Psychotherapy, whose German section is brought into line with the Nazi state. He said he took the post to protect Jewish members, but his statements and editing of its journal in these years remain controversial.
After a heart attack he has near-death visions he counted among the greatest experiences of his life. Psychology and Alchemy appears the same year.

history.what: The C. G. Jung Institute opens in Zurich
history.detail: Training in analytical psychology becomes formal.
Two of his most daring late works: one on meaningful coincidence, written alongside Pauli, and one arguing with God.
He dies on 6 June, ten days after finishing his chapter of Man and His Symbols.
After decades in a bank vault, Liber Novus appears in facsimile.

concepts.text: A layer of the psyche common to all humans.
concepts.detail: It is not shared memory. It is shared structure, as the body shares an anatomy. Jung inferred it from the recurrence of the same motifs in the dreams of modern people and in myths worldwide.
An archetype has no content of its own. It is like the axial system of a crystal, which shapes the crystal without being visible. We know archetypes only through the images they produce.

concepts.text: The unlived, unaccepted side of the personality.
concepts.detail: It contains what the ego rejects, including good qualities that were once unwelcome. It appears in dreams as a figure of the same sex and in waking life as the people we cannot stand.
A compromise between who one is and what society expects. Identification with it leaves a person brittle and empty.

concepts.text: The inner figure of the other.
concepts.detail: Jung described a feminine figure in men and a masculine one in women, mediating between ego and unconscious. Later Jungians have loosened the gendered scheme while keeping the idea of an inner counterpart.

concepts.text: The totality and the centre of the psyche.
concepts.detail: It appears in dreams as a circle, a square, a child, a wise figure, a jewel. Jung saw the God-images of the religions as its symbols.

concepts.text: The process of becoming an undivided person.
concepts.detail: Not individualism. Jung held that the more one becomes oneself, the more one is related to others, because projections fall away.
Introversion and extraversion describe where energy flows. Thinking, feeling, sensation and intuition describe how one orients. Everyone has a dominant function and a neglected, "inferior" one.
Jung’s example is a patient describing a dream of a golden scarab just as a scarab-like beetle taps at his window. He proposed that meaning can link events as cause does.

concepts.text: The alchemists projected the psyche into matter.
concepts.detail: Their operations, blackening, whitening, reddening and the marriage of opposites, describe stages of inner change. Jung spent thirty years on their texts.

facts.text: Jung built his tower at Bollingen without electricity or running water and kept it that way for life.
The Red Book stayed unpublished for forty-eight years after his death. Much of that time it lay in a Swiss bank vault.
The Myers-Briggs Type Indicator was developed from Jung’s Psychological Types by Katharine Briggs and Isabel Briggs Myers. Jung did not design it.
A letter from Jung to Bill Wilson in 1961 confirmed his part in the story behind Alcoholics Anonymous: he had told a patient that only a spiritual experience could help.
Over the door of his house at Küsnacht he carved, in Latin: called or not called, the god will be present.
He coined the words introvert, extravert, complex and synchronicity in their modern senses.
As a child he carved a small manikin, hid it in the attic with a painted stone, and told no one for decades.

glossary.meaning: Jung’s name for his school, to distinguish it from Freud’s psychoanalysis.
The "New Book": the formal title of the Red Book.
The village on Lake Zurich where Jung built his tower.
Annual conferences at Ascona where scholars of religion met from 1933.
The least developed of one’s four functions, and the doorway to the unconscious.

sensitivity.note: This Onda is self-observation, not psychotherapy. Jung’s methods can bring up strong material.
requiredCaveats: If you have a history of psychosis, dissociation or severe trauma, skip active imagination unless you are working with a clinician.
If what comes up is overwhelming or persistent, stop and contact a qualified therapist or Jungian analyst.
Some of Jung’s ideas about gender, culture and race reflect his time and have been criticised and revised.
